Q: Converting all text files with multiple encodings in a directory into a utf-8 encoded text files A:

Since in 2026 this is still a thing, specially for Open Data and Open Government Data, I used @jessica20119 's answer as a basis, and my final code is as follows:

The root folder is passed and all csv files in the directory and subdirectories are converted to a new file with its name indicating it is utf8.

def converter_utf8(diretorio_alvo):
    """
    Lista todos os arquivos de um diretório de forma recursiva.
    Converte os arquivos CSV para utf-8
    """
    caminho_base = Path(diretorio_alvo)
    conversoes = 0
    erros = 0
    
    if not caminho_base.exists() or not caminho_base.is_dir():
        print(f"Erro: O diretório '{diretorio_alvo}' não existe ou não é válido.")
        return

    print(f"=== Listando arquivos em: {caminho_base.resolve()} ===")
    
    # rglob('*') itera recursivamente em todos os itens da pasta
    for item in caminho_base.rglob('*'):
        if item.is_file():
            # resolve() retorna o caminho completo e absoluto
            arquivo_atual = item.resolve()

            # print(arquivo_atual)

            f = open(arquivo_atual, 'rb')
            data = f.read()
            f_charInfo = chardet.detect(data)
            coding = str(f_charInfo['encoding'])
            # coding=str(coding2)
            # print(f'arquivo: {arquivo_atual.name}, suffix: {arquivo_atual.suffix}, encoding: {coding}')

            # encoding_atual = ''
            encoding_destino = 'UTF-8'

                encoding_count[coding] += 1
            else:
                encoding_count[coding] = 1


            try:
                if (item.suffix == '.CSV' or item.suffix == '.csv') and not (coding == 'UTF-8' or coding == 'None'): 
                    print(f'convertendo arquivo: {arquivo_atual.name}, suffix: {arquivo_atual.suffix}, encoding: {coding}')
                    data = arquivo_atual.read_text(encoding=coding)

                    # arquivo_atual.write_text(data, encoding='utf-8')

                    arquivo_destino =  str(arquivo_atual).replace('.csv','_utf8.csv').replace('.CSV','_utf8.csv')

                    with open(arquivo_destino, 'w', encoding=encoding_destino) as outfile:
                        outfile.write(data)
                    
                    print(arquivo_destino)

                    # counting how many files were converted
                    conversoes += 1
            except PermissionError:
                print(f'Erro: Permissão negada para.{arquivo_atual}')
                erros += 1
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"Erro inesperado durante a varredura: {e}")
                erros += 1

    return {'conversoes': conversoes,'erros': erros}

Q: How do i fix the print code to give me the grades for 100 students instead of the 100th student A:

So it sounds like you didn't catch that a for loop in a prior cell would be independent from the following cells? If you are more used to developing in longer scripts, you can combine that kind of thing with notebook development by using %run -i my_script.py or %run my_script.py to run the script file code in or alongside, the notebook respectively. See more about the %run magic command here. (This special 'cell' situation to your code blocks additionally means that the information, "i use jupyter notes " would have been something to feature in the original post, or in the tags you added. You may wish to read How do I ask a good question? and use it as a guide going forward to making posts on StackOverflow.) I also sort of wondered if the last line of each cell in a Jupyter Notebooks being different than the earlier lines in that cell might have been contributing here? So I'll point out that typically, the expression on the last line of a cell gets evaluated and whatever that last expression would return is then displayed in the output area. You can though adjust that in Jupyter Notebooks, if you want, by running some code early in your notebook, see this answer to 'https://stackoverflow.com/a/36835741/8508004', and the comments below it. Since changing the interactivity may be unexpected by others & possibly confusing, to even yourself when you come back to the code much later, it may be best though to design in handling the various output streams like stderr and stdout, and not rely too much on the special property of the last line.

Q: Is compound assignment on atomic variables guaranteed to be atomic prior to C23? A:

§7.17.7.5 p5 was headed "Note", and in all ISO standards, notes aren't normative. So no implementer should ever have been using that paragraph to decide whether compound assignment operations should be atomic.

On the other hand, §6.5.16.2 p4 is normative, and states very clearly that compound assignment operators, applied to atomic types, operate atomically. So that's what implementers should have done.

I think the author of §7.17.7.5 p5 was trying to draw a comparison with compound assignment operators in general, as applied to types that are not necessarily atomic, which they probably thought would be more familiar to readers. Again, not as a way to define the behavior of atomic_fetch_* (because the paragraph is non-normative), but as an aid to understanding. It wasn't very successful, but I expect that implementers would nonetheless have understood in context what was meant, and wouldn't have been confused.

Certainly in the major implementations, the compound assignment operators, when applied to atomic types, have indeed acted as atomic read-modify-write operations, ever since the introduction of atomic types in C11. I think that is very safe to rely on (barring bugs, as always).

All that said, I would still prefer to use the atomic_fetch_* functions whenever possible: they make the atomic operation more explicit, and allow one to specify the memory ordering. Also, it's usually more useful to get the object's old value, rather than the new one.

There are a few odd instances where compound assignment permits an atomic operation for which there's no corresponding atomic_fetch_* function: *=, %=, <<=, etc.; but they're unlikely to be needed very often. Anyway, most architectures won't have machine instructions for those operations, so they'll be implemented with something like a compare-exchange loop; and so you might as well write such a loop explicitly in your source code. This has a bonus that it lets you choose the memory ordering. It would also make it easier to port to C++, which does not provide such operations on std::atomic types.

(In principle, a compiler could do a little better on an LL/SC machine, by actually doing the operation inside the LL/SC, but even state-of-the art C compilers currently don't do so: https://godbolt.org/z/sa47KnYvT .)
